I have 70 mu of land here in Quzhou, which is a lot more than most folks around me. I rent some of it from villagers who went to work in the cities. With only three people in my house—me, my wife, and our kid—I hire workers for harvest and transplanting, otherwise I could never manage it all. I have been doing this for six years now, since I was 41. Before that I worked in a factory in Handan, but I came back to farm because the money got better if you scale up.

My main system is still wheat-maize on 40 mu. That is my safe crop. Whatever happens, I can always sell wheat and maize, and the government buys wheat at a floor price, so I do not worry about losing everything. Last year on my wheat I used two bags of compound fertilizer per mu as base—each bag is 50 kg, so that is about 100 jin per mu—and then I topdressed with one bag of urea at jointing and half a bag at heading. It cost me money, but I got about 550 jin per mu, same as my neighbor Lao Wang. This year I will do the same. I do not want to risk cutting back on nitrogen because if the wheat turns yellow, I lose the whole year. I also irrigate four times: once after planting to help it settle for winter, once when it turns green in spring, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling. My well has enough water, but the electricity for the pump is expensive, so I do not water more than that.

For summer maize on those same 40 mu, I plant right after wheat harvest, usually around June 10th. I use a hybrid seed, Zhengdan 958, same as everyone else around here. I learned from the seed dealer that this variety is stable and the big farms all use it. For maize I put down one bag of compound fertilizer at planting and then side-dress urea when the plants are knee-high. I irrigate three times if it is dry—seedling stage, big trumpet stage, and when the grain is filling. Last year I got about 650 jin per mu. This year I expect the same.

Now for my cash crops. I plant 10 mu of watermelon because the profit is good if the price holds. I buy hybrid watermelon seedlings from the dealer in town—black-skinned varieties that the market likes. Watermelon needs a lot of potassium or the sweetness is no good. I put one and a half bags of compound fertilizer per mu as base, plus extra potassium sulfate, about half a bag per mu. I irrigate more often, maybe six times through the season, especially when the fruits are swelling. I spray pesticides five times because aphids and downy mildew always show up. I expect about 3,500 jin per mu if nothing goes wrong. I grow this on my sandy plot near the road because drainage is better there.

I have 10 mu of chili. Last year I made good money on chili, so I kept the area the same. I use an improved chili variety with thick walls that the vegetable buyers prefer. I transplant seedlings in late April or early May. For fertilizer, I give it similar to watermelon but a bit less potassium—still more than wheat though, because chili fruits need it. I irrigate five times and spray six times for mites and bacterial spot. I hope for around 1,800 jin per mu of fresh chili.

My cotton is 5 mu. I plant hybrid cotton. Cotton does not need as much water, so I irrigate three times—at planting, flowering, and boll opening. I fertilize with compound fertilizer as base and topdress a little urea at flowering. I spray four times for bollworm and aphids. I expect about 280 jin per mu of seed cotton. I keep this on the heavier soil plot.

I also have 5 mu of cauliflower. I plant a hybrid autumn cauliflower. It needs a lot of nitrogen and potassium to make big heads. I till the soil with a rotary tiller, put down plenty of base fertilizer with compost and compound fertilizer, and topdress twice. I irrigate four times and spray for cabbage worms and soft rot. I expect about 2,500 jin per mu.

I till the wheat land with a plough in autumn because wheat needs deep soil. For maize after wheat, I use rotary tillage to save time—I only have a few days between harvest and planting. For the vegetables and cotton I mostly use rotary tillage unless the land is too compacted.

I watch my neighbors closely. Last year, Old Zhang cut back on fertilizer to save money and his wheat yield dropped by 100 jin per mu. That taught me a lesson. I would rather spend an extra 100 yuan per mu on fertilizer than lose 500 yuan in grain. On a 70 mu farm, one bad decision hits hard. So I stick with what worked, adjust a little based on seed prices and fertilizer costs, and keep my eyes open.
